about: What real machines, and the people using them, showed must change in Windstorm Tardigrade, and the version each change is due in. A lesson here is a gate, not a note: tests/test_tardigrade.py (class Promises) refuses a version while a row due in it is not built, and refuses the version after it until the row says where it was proven on a real machine.
how_to_use: A new lesson gets a row the day it is learned: what was seen, the promise, a codon in DNA-STRAND-MASTER-PLAN.md, the version it is due in, and a tracking issue.
When it is built: put the name of its test in 'test'. The test must exist and be named in the plan next to the codon.
When it has been seen to work on a real machine: say which machine, which version and when in 'proven'.

'ship_in' moves only with a reason in 'moved_why'. A row whose owner is 'person' was seen by the person the skill is for, on his own machine: its date moves only by his word, restated in 'moved_by_person'.
A row is never deleted. A promise that turns out wrong is closed by a row that says why.
A lesson that was heard and not taken goes under 'declined' with the reason, so that nothing is dropped without a word.

rows.seen: 2026-11-21, the first real reboot of a shared machine with 98 sessions: sessions were started one at a time, about 11 seconds each, most of it waiting. The last was up 18 minutes after the first and 23 minutes after boot.
rows.promise: Sessions are started several at a time. The decision to start stays one by one, with a fresh look at what is running, so never a second copy still holds; only the waiting overlaps. How many at once is a setting, and load_max still applies.

rows.seen: 2026-11-21, the first real reboot of a shared machine with 98 sessions: every Herdr tab was attached in one block after the last session had started, 26 minutes after boot. Anyone who opened a tab before that saw an empty shell.
rows.promise: Each Herdr tab is attached as soon as its session is up, in the same pass as the trust answer and the note, not after all the starts.

rows.seen: 2026-11-21, the first real reboot of a shared machine with 98 sessions: nothing on the screen said that sessions were still coming back. The machine's owner looked 20 minutes after boot, took his session for lost and started a second copy of it by hand.
rows.promise: While a restore is running, the place where a session will appear says that it is on its way and how far the restore is (N of M), so nobody takes a session for lost and starts a second copy.

rows.seen: 2026-11-21, the first real reboot of a shared machine with 98 sessions: the only way to know a restore was still running was to read its log.
rows.promise: `census` says when a restore is running and how far it is. A desktop note says so when it starts and when it ends.

rows.seen: 2026-11-21, the first real reboot of a shared machine with 98 sessions: five Herdr workspaces did not come back with Herdr, so six sessions had no tab until a person made the workspaces again by hand.
rows.promise: A workspace that is gone is made again under its old name, with the tab in it: the person's layout is the thing to keep. A default workspace is used only if that fails.

rows.seen: The same night: two sessions carried one name, the real one and a copy started by hand. `revive --only NAME` matched both and started the copy its owner had just closed.
rows.promise: `revive --only` refuses a name that matches more than one session, lists their ids, and starts nothing.

rows.seen: The same night: a session its owner had ended with /exit two minutes earlier was still on the 5-minute record and was started again.
rows.promise: A session its owner ended is not brought back: its conversation ends with /exit, or its process is gone while its pane still holds the shell it left. A crash (G1.11) is never read as many sessions ended by hand.

rows.seen: 2026-11-21, the first real reboot of a shared machine with 98 sessions: a session started by hand during the restore, in the tab of a session that was coming back, was recorded as one more session under the same name. Nothing flagged it.
rows.promise: `census` names sessions that share a name, and marks a session that was started by hand in the place of one a restore was bringing back.

rows.seen: 2026-11-21, the first real reboot of a shared machine with 98 sessions: the timeline (boot, first start, last start, the count, the tabs, what went wrong) was pieced together from the log by hand, twice.
rows.promise: `report` prints the last restore's timeline and what still needs a person.

rows.seen: Switch day on that machine: so that setup's first record would not lose tab and workspace labels on a loaded machine, they were copied in by hand from the older tool's table.
rows.promise: setup's own record keeps every tab and workspace label it can read, and keeps the labels already on the record when Herdr is slow to answer.

rows.seen: The same night, for a second user of that machine whose sessions ran in plain terminal windows: they come back inside tmux with no window, and he has to know one command to see them.
rows.promise: On a desktop, a window opens by itself after login for each returned session that had a window, once the restore is done. A setting that setup offers; off where there is no desktop.

rows.seen: Before that reboot: finding which sessions were busy or had background commands that would be cut took a hand-written script and a message to every session.
rows.promise: `ready` says, before a planned reboot, which sessions are busy and which have background commands that will be cut.

rows.seen: 2026-11-21, the first real reboot of a shared machine with 98 sessions, as seen by the agent that runs that machine: all 98 sessions came back idle with nothing typed, as that machine was set. Their watchers and timers were gone, so nothing woke them: 70 minutes after boot only 9 had done anything, and the rest had to be messaged by hand. Each session's scratch folder under /tmp was gone too, with tools some of them relied on.
rows.promise: The wake-up note can be switched on for some sessions and not others (patterns in the settings), its words can be set, it says that /tmp was emptied, and on a machine with many sessions the notes are spaced so that they do not all take a turn in the same minute. It is typed only into an idle session with an empty box and no question open, as today.

rows.seen: 2026-11-21, the first real reboot of a shared machine with 98 sessions, as seen by the agent that runs that machine: a session's own posting tool and watcher lived under /tmp, which a reboot empties. They were gone and had to be rebuilt elsewhere.
rows.promise: `ready` names the sessions whose running background commands or scripts live under /tmp, because a reboot empties it.

rows.seen: 2026-11-21, the first real reboot of a shared machine with 98 sessions, as seen by the agent that runs that machine: the line with the counts went only to the log. The one responsible for the machine had to poll for it, or be woken from another machine.
rows.promise: With `on_done` set, that command is run when a restore ends, with the counts (started, loaded, not loaded, down, failed), so a person or a program is told instead of having to look.

rows.seen: 2026-11-21, the first real reboot of a shared machine with 98 sessions, as seen by the agent that runs that machine: switching the machine from its older restore tool meant finding every caller by hand: three units, a folder of scripts, a desktop icon, lines in other tools. The machine's own health check then failed twice because it knew sessions only by the old tool's command lines.
rows.promise: `setup` lists the other things on the machine that would start Claude sessions at boot or login (units, agents, autostart entries, desktop icons), so the person can switch them off: one restorer per session. It changes none of them.

rows.seen: 2026-11-21, the first real reboot of a shared machine with 98 sessions, as seen by the agent that runs that machine: making a missing Herdr workspace again opened an empty shell tab in it. Five such tabs were closed by hand, after checking each held nothing.
rows.promise: When a workspace is made again (G4.5), its blank first tab is used for the first session placed there, or closed if it holds nothing, so no empty tab is left.

rows.seen: 2026-11-21, the first real reboot of a shared machine with 98 sessions, as seen by the agent that runs that machine: `revive --only` for a running session printed only that it was already running, although it had also attached the session's tab.
rows.promise: `revive --only` says what it did about the session's tab: attached, already there, or left alone and why.

rows.seen: 2026-11-21, the first real reboot of a shared machine with 98 sessions, as seen by the agent that runs that machine: a timer its owner had stopped, but left enabled, started again at boot and had to be stopped before it fired. Another user timer, whose only trigger counted from its own last run, had no next run at all after the reboot until someone ran it once by hand.
rows.promise: `ready` lists this user's services and timers that a reboot will change: enabled but stopped now (they will start), running now but not enabled (they will not come back), and timers whose only trigger counts from their own last run (after a reboot they never fire again by themselves). It lists; it does not judge or change them.

rows.seen: 2026-11-21, the first real reboot of a shared machine with 98 sessions, as seen by the agent that runs that machine: the boot run began 4 minutes 35 seconds after boot, against about 2 minutes on a laptop, and the log does not say what it waited for.
rows.promise: The boot run logs how long after boot it began and what it waited for (its own fixed delay, the user's services coming up), and the progress line shows it.

rows.seen: 2026-11-21, the first real reboot of a shared machine with 98 sessions, as seen by the agent that runs that machine: a session started by hand in a plain shell was running, was not on the record, and nothing said that it would not survive a restart.
rows.promise: `census` marks each running session that is not on the record and says why (a pattern in the settings leaves it out, it is a helper of another session, it is newer than the last record), because such a session does not come back.

rows.seen: 2026-11-21, the first real reboot of a shared machine with 98 sessions, as seen by the agent that runs that machine: a second user's sessions were restored by his own install. The one responsible for the machine could confirm it only by counting processes from outside; reading the result would have meant entering his account.
rows.promise: Opt-in, off by default: after a restore the counts alone (started, loaded, down; no names, no folders) are written where other users of the machine can read them, so one person can confirm a restore for another without entering their account.

rows.seen: 2026-11-21, the first real reboot of a shared machine with 98 sessions, as seen by the agent that runs that machine: before the reboot every session was asked by hand, over messages, whether it was ready and what it would have to start again; after it, the ones with something to start again were messaged by hand.
rows.promise: `prep`: before a planned reboot each session is asked to write down what it must start again; the answers are kept with the record and given back to that session in its wake-up note. Asking a running session is a new kind of typing, so this needs its own invariant before it is built.

rows.seen: 2026-11-21, the first real reboot of a shared machine with 98 sessions, as seen by the agent that runs that machine: sessions that had been started with a name flag came back without it. Nothing broke, because a session keeps its title, but a start flag had been dropped without a word. Only the permission mode, the model, the effort and the added folders are carried today.
rows.promise: A session comes back with the start flags it had, all of them except the ones that name a conversation or pass a first message. A flag that cannot be carried is named in the log when the session is recorded, never dropped silently, and the README lists what is and is not carried.

declined.heard: 2026-11-21, the first real reboot of a shared machine with 98 sessions, as seen by the agent that runs that machine: two services of one of the machine's users both carried the same network tunnel, and the second looped on a failure to bind its port.
declined.why: Two services fighting over one thing is the machine's own configuration. Tardigrade will list a user's units that a reboot changes (G3.11); it does not judge whether two of them conflict.
